source: A day or two passed, and there was great activity aboard the Pequod. Not only were the old sails being mended, but new sails were coming on board, and bolts of canvas, and coils of rigging; in short, everything betokened that the ship’s preparations were hurrying to a close. Captain Peleg seldom or never went ashore, but sat in his wigwam keeping a sharp look-out upon the hands: Bildad did all the purchasing and providing at the stores; and the men employed in the hold and on the rigging were working till long after night-fall.

On the day following Queequeg’s signing the articles, word was given at all the inns where the ship’s company were stopping, that their chests must be on board before night, for there was no telling how soon the vessel might be sailing. So Queequeg and I got down our traps, resolving, however, to sleep ashore till the last. But it seems they always give very long notice in these cases, and the ship did not sail for several days. But no wonder; there was a good deal to be done, and there is no telling how many things to be thought of, before the Pequod was fully equipped.

Every one knows what a multitude of things—beds, sauce-pans, knives and forks, shovels and tongs, napkins, nut-crackers, and what not, are indispensable to the business of housekeeping. Just so with whaling, which necessitates a three-years’ housekeeping upon the wide ocean, far from all grocers, costermongers, doctors, bakers, and bankers. And though this also holds true of merchant vessels, yet not by any means to the same extent as with whalemen. For besides the great length of the whaling voyage, the numerous articles peculiar to the prosecution of the fishery, and the impossibility of replacing them at the remote harbors usually frequented, it must be remembered, that of all ships, whaling vessels are the most exposed to accidents of all kinds, and especially to the destruction and loss of the very things upon which the success of the voyage most depends. Hence, the spare boats, spare spars, and spare lines and harpoons, and spare everythings, almost, but a spare Captain and duplicate ship.

At the period of our arrival at the Island, the heaviest storage of the Pequod had been almost completed; comprising her beef, bread, water, fuel, and iron hoops and staves. But, as before hinted, for some time there was a continual fetching and carrying on board of divers odds and ends of things, both large and small.

Chief among those who did this fetching and carrying was Captain Bildad’s sister, a lean old lady of a most determined and indefatigable spirit, but withal very kindhearted, who seemed resolved that, if she could help it, nothing should be found wanting in the Pequod, after once fairly getting to sea. At one time she would come on board with a jar of pickles for the steward’s pantry; another time with a bunch of quills for the chief mate’s desk, where he kept his log; a third time with a roll of flannel for the small of some one’s rheumatic back. Never did any woman better deserve her name, which was Charity—Aunt Charity, as everybody called her. And like a sister of charity did this charitable Aunt Charity bustle about hither and thither, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised to yield safety, comfort, and consolation to all on board a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad was concerned, and in which she herself owned a score or two of well-saved dollars.

But it was startling to see this excellent hearted Quakeress coming on board, as she did the last day, with a long oil-ladle in one hand, and a still longer whaling lance in the other. Nor was Bildad himself nor Captain Peleg at all backward. As for Bildad, he carried about with him a long list of the articles needed, and at every fresh arrival, down went his mark opposite that article upon the paper. Every once in a while Peleg came hobbling out of his whalebone den, roaring at the men down the hatchways, roaring up to the riggers at the mast-head, and then concluded by roaring back into his wigwam.

During these days of preparation, Queequeg and I often visited the craft, and as often I asked about Captain Ahab, and how he was, and when he was going to come on board his ship. To these questions they would answer, that he was getting better and better, and was expected aboard every day; meantime, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could attend to everything necessary to fit the vessel for the voyage. If I had been downright honest with myself, I would have seen very plainly in my heart that I did but half fancy being committed this way to so long a voyage, without once laying my eyes on the man who was to be the absolute dictator of it, so soon as the ship sailed out upon the open sea. But when a man suspects any wrong, it sometimes happens that if he be already involved in the matter, he insensibly strives to cover up his suspicions even from himself. And much this way it was with me. I said nothing, and tried to think nothing.
At last it was given out that some time next day the ship would certainly sail. So next morning, Queequeg and I took a very early start.

modern_en.title: Chapter 20 — All Astir
paragraphs: A day or two passed, and there was great activity aboard the Pequod. Old sails were being mended, new sails were coming on board, along with bolts of canvas and coils of rigging. Everything indicated that the ship's preparations were hurrying to a close. Captain Peleg seldom or never went ashore, but sat in his wigwam keeping a sharp eye on the crew. Bildad handled all the purchasing and provisioning at the shops. And the men working in the hold and up in the rigging kept at it long after dark.

The day after Queequeg signed the articles, word was sent to all the inns where the crew was staying that their sea chests had to be on board before nightfall — there was no telling how soon the ship might sail. So Queequeg and I brought our belongings down, though we planned to sleep ashore until the last possible night. But it seems they always give very long notice in these cases, and the ship didn't actually sail for several more days. No surprise there — there was a great deal to be done, and no telling how many details needed attending to before the Pequod was fully equipped.

Everyone knows what a multitude of things — beds, saucepans, knives and forks, shovels and tongs, napkins, nutcrackers, and whatnot — are indispensable for running a household. It's just the same with whaling, which requires three years of housekeeping on the open ocean, far from all grocers, costermongers (street sellers of fruit and vegetables), doctors, bakers, and bankers. This is true of merchant ships too, but nowhere near to the same extent as with whalers. Besides the great length of the voyage and the many specialized items needed for the whale hunt, and the impossibility of replacing them at the remote harbors these ships usually visit, you have to remember that of all ships, whalers are the most exposed to accidents of every kind — especially the destruction and loss of the very equipment on which the voyage's success depends. Hence the spare boats, spare spars, spare lines and harpoons, and spare almost everything — everything but a spare captain and a duplicate ship.

By the time we arrived at the island, most of the Pequod's heavy stores had already been loaded — her beef, bread, water, fuel, iron hoops, and barrel staves. But as I mentioned, there was a constant stream of odds and ends, both large and small, being carried on board.

Chief among those doing this ferrying was Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady of fierce and tireless determination, but genuinely kindhearted. She seemed resolved that, if she had anything to say about it, nothing would be found lacking on the Pequod once the ship was fairly at sea. One time she came aboard with a jar of pickles for the steward's pantry. Another time with a bunch of quill pens for the chief mate's desk, where he kept his log. Another with a roll of flannel for the small of someone's rheumatic back. No woman ever better deserved her name, which was Charity — Aunt Charity, as everyone called her. And like a sister of charity, this charitable Aunt Charity bustled here and there, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised safety, comfort, or consolation to everyone aboard a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad had an interest, and in which she herself owned a score or two of well-saved dollars.

But it was startling to see this kind-hearted Quaker woman come aboard on the last day carrying a long oil ladle in one hand and an even longer whaling lance in the other. Nor were Bildad and Captain Peleg any less busy. Bildad carried a long checklist of needed supplies, and at every delivery, he made a mark next to that item on his list. Every now and then, Peleg hobbled out of his whalebone den, roaring at the men down the hatchways, roaring up at the riggers on the masthead, and then concluded by roaring back into his wigwam.

During these days of preparation, Queequeg and I often visited the ship, and each time I asked about Captain Ahab — how he was and when he planned to come aboard. They always answered that he was getting better and better and was expected any day. In the meantime, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could handle everything needed to ready the vessel. If I had been truly honest with myself, I would have seen plainly that I only half liked the idea of being committed to such a long voyage without once laying eyes on the man who would be its absolute dictator the moment the ship reached open sea. But when a man suspects something is wrong, it sometimes happens that, if he is already caught up in the matter, he unconsciously tries to cover up his suspicions even from himself. And that's exactly what I did. I said nothing and tried to think nothing.
At last the word came that the ship would definitely sail the next day. So the following morning, Queequeg and I got a very early start.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 20 — Alle på færde
paragraphs: Der gik en dag eller to, og der var stor travlhed om bord på Pequod. Gamle sejl blev repareret, nye sejl kom om bord sammen med baller af lærred og ruller af rigning. Alt tydede på, at skibets forberedelser skyndte sig mod deres afslutning. Kaptajn Peleg gik sjældent eller aldrig i land, men sad i sin wigwam og holdt et vågent øje med mandskabet. Bildad stod for alle indkøb og proviantering i butikkerne. Og mændene, der arbejdede i lasten og oppe i rigningen, blev ved længe efter mørkets frembrud.

Dagen efter at Queequeg havde skrevet under på kontrakten, blev der sendt besked til alle de værtshuse, hvor mandskabet boede, om at deres sømandskister skulle være om bord inden aften — man vidste ikke, hvor snart skibet kunne sejle. Så Queequeg og jeg bragte vores ejendele ned, selv om vi havde tænkt os at sove i land til den allersidste mulige nat. Men det ser ud til, at de altid giver meget langt varsel i sådanne tilfælde, og skibet sejlede faktisk ikke før adskillige dage efter. Det er der ikke noget at sige til — der var meget at gøre, og man kunne ikke vide, hvor mange enkeltheder der skulle ordnes, før Pequod var fuldt udrustet.

Alle ved, hvilken mængde ting — senge, kasseroller, knive og gafler, skovle og ildtænger, servietter, nøddeknækkere og hvad ved jeg — der er uundværlige for at drive en husholdning. Det er netop det samme med hvalfangst, der kræver tre års husholdning på åbent hav, langt fra alle købmænd, gadesælgere (folk, der sælger frugt og grønt på gaden), læger, bagere og bankfolk. Det gælder også for handelsskibe, men slet ikke i nær samme grad som for hvalfangere. Ud over rejsens store længde og de mange særlige genstande, som hvaljagten kræver, og umuligheden i at erstatte dem i de afsidesliggende havne, som disse skibe som regel besøger, skal man huske, at hvalfangere af alle skibe er de mest udsatte for ulykker af enhver art — især ødelæggelse og tab af netop det udstyr, som rejsens held afhænger af. Derfor de ekstra både, ekstra rundholter, ekstra liner og harpuner og ekstra næsten alt — alt undtagen en ekstra kaptajn og et dobbelt skib.

Da vi nåede øen, var det meste af Pequods tunge forsyninger allerede læsset — hendes oksekød, brød, vand, brændsel, jernbånd og tøndestave. Men som jeg nævnte, var der en uafbrudt strøm af alskens ting, store og små, som blev båret om bord.

Den vigtigste af dem, der stod for denne transport, var kaptajn Bildads søster, en tynd gammel dame med hård og utrættelig beslutsomhed, men virkelig godhjertet. Hun syntes fast besluttet på, at hvis hun skulle have noget at sige, skulle intet mangle på Pequod, når skibet først var ordentligt til søs. Én gang kom hun om bord med en krukke pickles til stewardens spisekammer. En anden gang med et bundt fjerpenne til førstestyrmandens skrivebord, hvor han førte sin logbog. En anden med en rulle flonel til lænden på en eller anden med gigt. Ingen kvinde har nogensinde bedre fortjent sit navn, som var Charity — tante Charity, som alle kaldte hende. Og som en barmhjertighedssøster fór denne barmhjertige tante Charity rundt, rede til at give hånd og hjerte til alt, der lovede sikkerhed, trøst eller lindring for alle om bord på et skib, hvori hendes elskede bror Bildad havde en andel, og hvori hun selv ejede en snes velopsparede dollars.

Men det var forbløffende at se denne godhjertede kvækerkvinde komme om bord på den sidste dag med en lang transke i den ene hånd og en endnu længere hvalfangerlanse i den anden. Bildad og kaptajn Peleg var heller ikke mindre travle. Bildad bar på en lang liste over nødvendige varer, og ved hver levering satte han et mærke ved den vare på sin liste. Hvert øjeblik humpede Peleg ud af sin hvalbensgrotte, brølede ned ad lugerne til mændene, brølede op til rigningsfolkene i mastetoppen og sluttede med at brøle sig tilbage ind i sin wigwam.

I disse forberedelsesdage besøgte Queequeg og jeg ofte skibet, og hver gang spurgte jeg efter kaptajn Ahab — hvordan han havde det, og hvornår han agtede at komme om bord. De svarede altid, at han blev bedre og bedre og ventedes hver dag. I mellemtiden kunne de to kaptajner, Peleg og Bildad, klare alt, hvad der skulle til for at gøre fartøjet klar. Hvis jeg havde været helt ærlig over for mig selv, ville jeg tydeligt have set, at jeg kun halvt brød mig om tanken om at binde mig til sådan en lang rejse uden så meget som én gang at have lagt øjne på den mand, der ville blive dens enevældige diktator, så snart skibet nåede åbent hav. Men når en mand har en mistanke om, at noget er galt, sker det somme tider, at hvis han allerede er viklet ind i sagen, forsøger han ubevidst at skjule sin mistanke selv for sig selv. Og det er præcis, hvad jeg gjorde. Jeg sagde intet og prøvede ikke at tænke noget.
Til sidst kom beskeden om, at skibet helt sikkert ville sejle næste dag. Så næste morgen kom Queequeg og jeg meget tidligt afsted.
